name: Whey isolate

lead: Whey isolate is whey protein that has been filtered further than concentrate so that fat and lactose are largely removed, leaving protein of typically over 90% by dry weight. People use it as a shake or in recipes to reach protein targets while training, which supports muscle building and, through that, a more muscular physique.

Research on whey and training is broad; an 11-week trial in resistance-trained men tested whey alongside creatine, and a small 12-week pilot tested whey isolate against placebo with ultrasound muscle thickness. A 2010 EFSA review described whey as about as effective for strength and lean mass as other protein sources.

paras: Powder is mixed with water or milk, commonly around workouts or as a meal supplement, and combined with resistance training. Gains build over weeks of training.

Whey is a milk product; people with milk allergy are affected, and isolate is lower in lactose than concentrate. Very high protein intakes are discussed with clinicians for people with kidney conditions.

web.title: ISSN position stand: diets and body composition
ISSN position stand: protein and exercise

chain: Whey isolate supplies protein after training
Supports muscle protein synthesis and recovery
More muscle mass over training months
angle.text: Lifters use whey isolate to reach daily protein targets, which supports the muscle growth they build through training. It delivers protein with little fat or lactose, which suits people managing calories while trying to stay lean and keep muscle.

lead: Whey isolate is whey protein processed to remove most fat and lactose, typically reaching over 90% protein by dry weight.[1] People use it as a convenient protein powder alongside resistance training: more protein through the day supports muscle repair and growth, and more muscle over months of training shows up as a fuller, more muscular and often leaner-looking physique.[2]

Whey is the liquid left over from cheese making and is purified by membrane filtration or ion exchange, then spray-dried.[1] It is one of three common whey forms: concentrate (some fat and lactose remain), isolate, and hydrolysate (partly pre-digested).[1][3] Sports nutrition position statements describe whey as fast-digesting and rich in leucine and essential amino acids, and in the studies they review it stimulated muscle protein synthesis more than casein or soy.[2]

In a double-blind 11-week trial of resistance-trained men, supplementation with whey and/or creatine produced greater strength gains than carbohydrate in several lifts.[4] A small 12-week pilot compared whey isolate with an isocaloric placebo for muscle thickness and strength.[5] A 2010 European Food Safety Authority opinion described whey as about as effective as other protein sources for strength, muscle and lean mass.[1]
infobox: Membrane filtration (micro-/ultrafiltration, diafiltration) or ion exchange[1]
Food supplement; US makers need not prove safety to FDA before sale[3]

paras: Whey makes up roughly 20% of cow's milk protein, with casein making up the other 80%.[1] The main whey proteins are beta-lactoglobulin (about 65%), alpha-lactalbumin (about 25%), bovine serum albumin and immunoglobulins.[1]

Isolate is made from whey by filtration steps that remove fat, lactose and minerals; concentrate retains more of each.[1] Microfiltration removes bacteria, casein micelles and fat, ultrafiltration keeps the proteins, and diafiltration (adding water during ultrafiltration) strips more lactose and minerals. Ion-exchange chromatography is another major route.[1] Concentrates range from roughly 29 to 89% protein, isolates are 90% or more, and hydrolysates are pre-digested for faster absorption at higher cost.[3]

In the late 1960s, surplus whey was an economic and environmental problem for New Zealand's dairy industry. In 1969 Coca-Cola sought a soluble whey protein for acidic drinks, and New Zealand researchers produced a 65% protein concentrate by ultrafiltration in 1970.[1] Coca-Cola launched the whey-fortified drink Tai in Brazil in 1971, and Alex Malaspina and Roberto Moretti patented an acid-soluble, low-mineral process in 1975.[1]

Protein powders for lifters predate whey: in the 1950s Irvin P. Johnson began marketing egg-based protein powders to bodybuilders, and the supplement industry grew rapidly in the 1970s and 1980s.[3] The US Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 moved responsibility for supplement safety to manufacturers rather than pre-market FDA approval.[3] New Zealand formed the Whey Products Corporation in 1982, and its dairy board later merged into Fonterra in 2001.[1]

Bodybuilders favour protein powders because they are convenient, cheaper than meat or fish and quick to prepare; they are usually mixed with water, milk or juice and taken around workouts or in place of a meal.[3] Whey is rich in branched-chain amino acids and has the highest cysteine content of common proteins.[3]

The International Society of Sports Nutrition's 2017 position stand on protein and exercise says about 1.4 to 2.0 g of protein per kg of body weight per day is sufficient for most exercising people to build or maintain muscle, with roughly 0.25 g/kg (20 to 40 g) per serving and even spacing across the day. It adds that total daily intake appears to matter more than precise timing, and that supplements are a practical way to reach targets while limiting calories.[2] A companion position stand on diets and body composition says that for lean, resistance-trained people in a calorie deficit, higher intakes of 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of fat-free mass may help preserve lean mass.[6]

General nutrition references note that people eating balanced diets do not need protein supplements; whey is one of several convenient sources alongside casein, egg, soy and rice proteins.[7] Wikipedia's whey article states that taking whey before exercise does not improve athletic performance, and that its main claimed use is muscle growth and recovery after training.[1]

An EFSA review in 2010 found whey about as effective as other protein sources for strength and lean mass, and found no evidence supporting weight-loss claims.[1] The ISSN position stand describes whey as producing stronger muscle protein synthesis responses than casein and soy in the studies it cites, while noting plant proteins can work at larger doses or in combination.[2] Trials of whey with training in resistance-trained adults are described under Clinical studies.[4][5]

Whey proteins cause some milk allergies, although caseins are the major milk allergens; highly hydrolysed whey may be less allergenic.[1] Isolate has less lactose than concentrate, which is why people with lactose sensitivity sometimes choose it.[1][3]

Supplement quality has drawn media and regulatory attention. In 2015 Consumer Reports reported arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury in several protein powders it tested, and a 2015 CBC investigation reported protein spiking with amino-acid filler; many companies disputed these findings.[3] Because US makers need not show safety evidence to the FDA before marketing, label accuracy depends on manufacturer practices, and some consumers look for third-party testing seals.[3]

A randomized trial in resistance-trained males tested whey, creatine, both, or carbohydrate over 11 weeks of training, measuring strength, DEXA body composition and muscle biopsy fibre size; the whey, creatine and combination groups improved 1RM strength more than the carbohydrate group in several lifts.[4] A blinded pilot trial gave 4 participants whey isolate and 4 an isocaloric placebo for 12 weeks of resistance training, with ultrasound muscle thickness, isokinetic strength and body composition measured.[5]
Position stands from the International Society of Sports Nutrition review the broader trial literature on protein intake and body composition.[6][2]

lore.intro: Whey isolate is discussed in lifting communities as the default clean protein powder, often compared with concentrate and with plant proteins.
